title: NVMe & Storage Protocols
summary: Why NVMe replaced AHCI/SATA once the storage medium itself got fast enough to expose the protocol as the bottleneck.

slides.sectionTitle: When storage got faster than its protocol
slides.markdown:
**SATA/AHCI** was designed in an era when the disk itself — a spinning HDD taking milliseconds per access — was always the bottleneck. A single command queue and a handful of microseconds of protocol overhead were irrelevant next to multi-millisecond seek times ([hdd-mechanics-and-performance](hdd-mechanics-and-performance)).

Once SSDs made flash access latency drop to **microseconds**, that assumption flipped: the protocol's own overhead — command queuing, interrupt handling, the single-queue design — became large enough *relative to the device* to matter. AHCI wasn't broken; it was simply built for a world where the device was always slower than the interface talking to it.

**NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express)** is a protocol designed from scratch for flash, built to talk to storage directly over **PCIe** rather than through the legacy SATA/AHCI stack originally designed for spinning disks.

By skipping the translation layers AHCI needed to stay compatible with decades of disk-oriented software, NVMe cuts per-command overhead dramatically and lets the storage device's own speed — not the protocol wrapped around it — set the ceiling on performance.

AHCI supports exactly **one command queue** with a depth of 32 commands — a design matched to a single mechanical device that could only really be doing one thing at a time anyway.

NVMe supports up to **65,535 queues**, each holding up to **65,536 commands**. This isn't over-engineering: an SSD's internal flash is made of many independent channels/dies that can genuinely service requests in parallel, and NVMe's queue depth is what lets software actually keep all of that internal parallelism busy instead of starving it through one narrow queue.

Laid out side by side, the queue-depth difference explains most of NVMe's throughput advantage on modern SSDs.

![AHCI's single command queue versus NVMe's many parallel submission/completion queue pairs feeding a multi-channel SSD](assets/nvme-vs-ahci-queues.svg)

AHCI's one queue forces every command through a single choke point regardless of how parallel the underlying flash is; NVMe's many queues (often one per CPU core) let requests reach the device in parallel, matching software parallelism to hardware parallelism.

assets.alt: AHCI's single command queue versus NVMe's many parallel submission/completion queue pairs feeding a multi-channel SSD

slides.markdown:
The two protocols diverge sharply on the metrics that matter once the storage device itself is fast.

| | SATA/AHCI | NVMe |
|---|---|---|
| Queues | 1 | Up to 65,535 |
| Queue depth | 32 commands | Up to 65,536 per queue |
| Typical link | SATA (~600 MB/s ceiling) | PCIe (multi-GB/s, scales with lanes/gen) |
| Interrupt handling | Higher relative overhead | Streamlined for high IOPS |

For an HDD or an older, slower SSD, this difference barely registers — but for a fast NVMe-class SSD, AHCI's single queue and interrupt overhead would throttle the device well below its real capability.

A common mix-up is treating **NVMe** as if it were a physical connector standard — like calling something "an NVMe port." NVMe is a **protocol** (a command set and queueing model), not a physical interface.

It happens to most commonly run over **PCIe** (via M.2 or U.2 connectors), but it can also run over a network entirely — **NVMe-oF (NVMe over Fabrics)** carries the same protocol over Ethernet, Fibre Channel, or InfiniBand to talk to remote storage with far lower overhead than older network storage protocols. Confusing the protocol with its most common physical carrier hides that NVMe-oF exists at all.
